## ABSTRACT

Detailed experimental and computational information on the response of lithium surfaces to irradiation by slow hydrogenic particles (ions, atoms, molecules) is sparse and mainly speculative. In this work, we present a computational study of the reflection and retention of deuterium (D) atoms at crystalline and amorphous lithium surfaces at 300 and 500 K, where the D atoms have an impact energy in the range of 0.025–5 eV and incident angles of 0° (perpendicular incidence) or 85° (near-grazing incidence). Classical molecular dynamics simulations are performed with the reactive bond-order force field (ReaxFF) potentials. This study provides quantitative information on the deuterium sticking probability and recycling coefficient for lithium surfaces. Our results support the ongoing work at the Lithium Tokamak eXperiment-β fusion experiment as well as relevant experiments in the laboratory setting.

I. INTRODUCTION

The use of lithium as a plasma-facing material has been investigated in various devices such as the Lithium Tokamak eXperiment (LTX),1 National Spherical Torus eXperiment (NSTX),2 EAST,3

HIDRA,4 and STOR-M.5 Researchers at LTX at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory reported improved plasma performance and a flat electron temperature profile due to a lowering of the hydrogen recycling coefficient (Rw), which is the ratio of the flux of ejected hydrogen atoms from the wall to the flux of incident hydrogen ions and atoms from the plasma.1,6 Hydrogen recycling at Li plasma-facing components is a complex function of many variables including the Li oxidation state, uptake of H in the Li surface, surface temperature of the wall, and incident energy of hydrogen.7–13

There is still much to be learned about the plasma–material interactions at Li surfaces in order to optimize plasma performance. The electron temperature in LTX plasmas reaches 100–300 eV in the core and into the edge, although neutral gas temperatures (Tg) near the edge are closer to the wall temperature (<1000 K).14

In the neutral gas temperature range Tg < 1 eV, which is typical in fusion devices, lithium readily absorbs atomic hydrogen much more than diatomic hydrogen because for diatomic hydrogen to be

absorbed in lithium, it must dissociate into atomic hydrogen.15 The bond dissociation energy of H2 is 4.5 eV,16 making non-catalytic dissociation unlikely for H2 impacts at Tg < 1 eV. The kinetics of hydrogen sorption by lithium typically involves the sticking coefficient, which is defined as

S(E, θ, T) ¼ NS(E, θ, T) Ni(E, θ) , (1)

where NS is the number of particles retained by the lithium surface, Ni is the number of impacting particles at the surface, E is the incident energy, θ is the incident angle, and T is the surface temperature.17–22 It is important to define the surface as the transition region between the material bulk and the vacuum, which could have a thickness from nm to μm, depending on the observed process and particle incident energy. It is important to distinguish the structure of lithium as amorphous (solid or liquid) or crystalline in order to establish possible roles that the Li surface structure can play in hydrogen recycling. Due to the large particle fluxes and wide energy and angular ranges of particles irradiating the walls in a fusion reactor, it is commonly

Thus, on a microscopic scale relevant to this work, the surface of the lithium deposited inside fusion devices is expected to be amorphous, consisting of peaks and valleys at nm to μm scales due to the roughness of an underlying solid substrate or deposition, ejection, and bubble formation mechanisms of liquid metals.23,24

Amorphous systems can possess spatial variability in bond parameters, leading to local differences in surface reactivity.25 For those reasons, we selected an amorphous Li surface as our primary target, although we also report herein studies of D atom interactions with a pristine crystalline surface. Tokamak divertors typically employ grazing incident angles of the magnetic field at the surface (≈90° from the surface normal). Hence, H atoms can also be anisotropically oriented to a grazing incidence angle due to charge exchange reactions with ions, which move toward the surface in a gyro motion along the B-field. This anisotropic velocity distribution of H atoms and the surface roughness gives rise to a variety of incident angles of H atoms impinging at the surface. The molecular dynamics (MD) method used in this work to simulate the irradiation process of atomic deuterium on amorphous and crystalline lithium surfaces is briefly described in Sec. II. Our results are presented and discussed in Sec. III. Finally, our conclusions are provided in Sec. IV.

II. COMPUTATIONAL METHOD

Modeling was done by implementing the bond order-based force field ReaxFF26 in the molecular dynamics simulator LAMMPS (LargeScale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator).27 Due to the large difference in the electronegativities of Li (0.98) and H (2.2),28,29 the bonding between Li and H is mixed ionic-covalent, which is carefully taken into account by ReaxFF. This approach to modeling Li-H systems was verified in previous research performed by Krstić et al.30–33 The simulations presented in this work utilized one of two different Li surface targets: (1) a slab with a monocrystalline BCC structure [Li(100) surface34]; lattice constant 3.609 Å or (2) a slab with an amorphous

structure. The crystalline slab, after 3D energy minimization, thermalization to the surface temperatures (TLi) of 300 and 500 K, and relaxation to the surface boundary conditions and 2D periodicity, occupied a box of approximate dimensions 7.8 × 7.8 × 2 nm3, containing 5000 7Li atoms (Fig. 1). Amorphization of the crystalline slab was done using the usual procedure, by repeatedly fast heating to 5000 K and slow annealing to 300 K with 3D periodicity, followed by relaxation to the surface boundary conditions and 2D periodicity (in the x- and y-directions). The final bounding box of the amorphous slab at 300 K had approximate dimensions of 8 × 8 × 2 nm3 and contained 5000 atoms. The mass densities of both crystalline and amorphous slabs were about 0.5 g/cm3, close to the densities of bulk solid and liquid lithium. The surface was thermalized as a NVE (microcanonical) ensemble by a Langevin thermostat with a time constant of 100 fs. In the following discussions, we will utilize the nomenclature c:Li and a:Li as shorthand for the crystalline Li surface and the amorphous Li surface, respectively. The Lindeman index17 of the considered Li slabs was calculated over 5000 one-fs steps at 300 and 400 K (crystalline surface) and 500 and 600 K (amorphous surface) (see Fig. 2). The sharp increase in the Lindemann index between 400 and 500 K indicates the typical phase transition for Li from solid to liquid between 400 and 500 K (Li melting point is 453 K at 1 atm). A commonly accepted criterion for a liquid phase is a Lindemann index of  0:1, which is approximately achieved (>0.07) in spite of our relatively small slab. We will consider the results obtained with 500 K amorphous lithium surfaces as valid for liquid Li. In Sec. III, we also provide results for amorphous and crystalline Li slabs at 300 K. We examined the H impact energy (E) range of 0.025–5 eV, which is relevant for tokamak reactors, and impact angles (θ) of 0° and 85° (measured from the surface normal) to investigate the sensitivity of H sticking on the impact angle. Chemical sputtering can occur at lower energies through a sequence of chemical reactions that create weakly bonded particles, which are easily expelled from the material.13 However, chemical sputtering from a Li surface by incident D occurs at impact energies within those utilized in this study (0.03–5 eV) and was not observed in our results, indicating that the sputtering probability is negligibly small (≤0.1%) in the considered energy range with 1023 impact trajectories. In the case of crystalline Li (100), this is in concurrence with Li on Li adsorption energies in the range of −0.9 to −1.33 eV, as calculated by Gaissmaier et al.34

Given a set of input parameters, including θ and E, individual runs were performed with deuterium atoms impacting the surface, scanning the surface uniformly with N = 1023 trajectories at different impact points (x, y) for each particle. The data from each trajectory were collected and analyzed for each input set. If Ns is the number of successful trajectories (Ns ≤N) and n is a sampled size of desired outcome O, then the probability of O per impact atom is PO = nO/Ns, with a standard error SEO given by SEO ¼ PO/ ﬃﬃﬃﬃ no p .18

So, the reflection probability is PR = nR/Ns, while the probability of sticking [Eq. (1)] of D per impact is Pret = 1 −PR. The size of a time step in MD depends primarily on the impact energy. For the very small impact energies considered in this work, the time step of 1 fs for E  0:1 eV and 0.5 fs for E > 0.1 eV was satisfactory. The number of time steps per single trajectory depends on both the impact energy and the incident angle. Since all trajectories have started from about 1 nm above the surface, the number of time steps steeply increased with incident angle. For θ = 85°, the number of time steps for an impact energy of 0.05 eV was typically 8000. The needed number of steps increases steeply with a further increase in the incident angle, which becomes computationally formidable. However, for orthogonal impact (θ = 0°), the typical number of time steps was about 3000 at E = 0.05 eV. In the case of singly charged ions impinging on a metal surface, it is assumed that the ions are neutralized at asymptotic distances by electrons from the Fermi sea of the metal target before reaching the surface. Consequently, impacts of neutral D atoms effectively capture the behavior of impinging D ions, as confirmed by a number of experiments.7,9,10,17,18 Our calculations assumed a single atom hitting a surface. No effects due to the accumulation of D at the surface were taken into account, which will be a subject of our future studies.

III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

As discussed in Sec. II, the probabilities of reflection (PR) are calculated for each impact energy and incident angle as a ratio of the number of reflected trajectories (NR) and the total number of successful trajectories (NS), with PR = NR/NS. The probabilities of sticking (retention) per D impact, Pret, are in all cases defined by particle conservation, i.e., Pret= 1 −PR, and therefore do not need to be separately discussed.

(∼290 K, see the temperature scale given at the top of Fig. 3) to 5 eV (∼58 000 K). According to the discussion of the Lindemann index in Sec. II, the 500 K amorphous Li slab may be interpreted as a liquid Li surface. For the 300 K slab in Fig. 3(a), D at perpendicular and grazing incident angles shows a significant difference (up to 3–4 times) in reflection probability only for E > 1 eV. For the 500 K slab in Fig. 3(b), D at grazing incidence shows a higher PR than at perpendicular incidence for the entirety of the considered energy range, with differences increasing from about 2.5 to 4 times as the impact energy increases. On the other hand, comparing the PR values for TLi of 300 and 500 K, the reflection probabilities are persistently larger at the higher lithium surface temperature, irrespective of the impact energy and incident angle. However, this difference decreases with increasing E, and at E = 5 eV, PR at 300 K exceeds that at 500 K. Thus, for θ = 0°, PR(TLi = 300 K, E = 25 meV) = 0.6%, while PR(TLi = 500 K, E = 25 meV) = 1.7%. The difference between PR values at the two Li surface temperatures diminishes as E ≥0.1 eV, as illustrated in Fig. S1 in the supplementary material.

A quantum-mechanical calculation of the reflection of the impact D atoms from c:Li might reveal Bragg-like diffraction structures in the angular distributions.35 These diffraction structures could appear in the lower range of the considered impact energies, for which the de Broglie wavelength of D is comparable to the Li lattice constant. These effects are not accessible in the present classical consideration. We also calculated the depth distribution of the D atoms that were retained in a:Li at 300 K for various impact energies and incident angles (Fig. 6). At perpendicular incidence (θ = 0°), 95% of the retained D atoms with E = 0.1 eV accumulated at depths shallower than 7.4 Å from the vacuum interface (0 Å depth) as shown in Fig. 6(a), and the distribution of these D atoms, as shown in Fig. 6(b) for the same case, is symmetric with a peak at 3.2 Å. The peak positions for the distributions shown in Fig. 6(b) do not change much with increasing impact energy, but the widths of the

peaks expand toward deeper depths. The peak position for the depth distribution from perpendicular D atoms incident at E = 3 eV is at a depth of about 4 Å, but incident D is retained deeper in the surface with 95% of the retained D atoms at depths shallower than 13 Å. For grazing incidence (θ = 85°), as shown in Fig. 6(c), 95% of the retained D atoms were retained at depths shallower than 4.7 Å for E = 0.1 eV and at depths shallower than 10 Å for E = 3 eV. Interestingly, as shown in Fig. 6(d), the peak of the distribution for E = 0.1 eV is at about 1.5 Å above the vacuum interface, showing a significant “accumulation” of D as adatoms above the first Li layer. This adatom peak is present for all considered impact energies in Fig. 6(d). However, as the impact energy increases, the adatom peak counts decrease and the dominant peak for the distributions is shifted beneath the surface and occurs at a depth of 3.3 Å below the vacuum interface for E = 1 eV and at 4.2 Å for E = 3 eV. Most of the retained D atoms appear below the vacuum interface, even for almost grazing incidence at θ = 85°.

IV. CONCLUSIONS

In this work, we utilized molecular dynamics simulations to study the sticking probability of incident D atoms (E = 0.025–5 eV; θ = 0° or 85° measured from the surface normal) on crystalline and amorphous Li surfaces at 300 or 500 K. Our results revealed slightly higher reflection probabilities (and lower sticking probabilities) for deuterium at lithium surfaces in an amorphous (liquid) lithium state (500 K), which can be expected in fusion devices, in comparison to the amorphous solid lithium surface at room temperature. This difference is particularly present at the lowest impact energies (0.025 eV, 300 K) and at a grazing incidence angle. The crystalline and amorphous surfaces do not show significant differences in the sticking and reflection of D atoms if the other conditions of impact angle and Li surface temperature are the same. Energy distributions of the reflected D atoms are linearly dependent on the impact energy, with the gradient (0.25–0.5) mainly dependent on the D incident angle. The average reflected angle of D atoms is spread between 40° and 65° for all considered parameters of the surface and irradiating particles. The D atoms retained in lithium in these simulations are distributed within a few surface monolayers, with the depth strongly depending on the impact angle and energy. The formation of a D adatom layer is predicted for D irradiation at grazing incidence θ = 85°, but the details of this would strongly depend on the accumulation of D in Li. The deuterization of the Li surface could have significant consequences on its physicochemical properties, as has been shown in the past for other materials.36–40 This would certainly influence the retention and reflection of D as well as erosion of the Li surface and will be a subject of our future research.
